questions.question: A cold virus left on a doorknob sticks to a girl's fingers as she opens the door. A few days later she comes down with a cold. Where did the virus most likely get into her body?
choices: The lining inside her nose
The pores of her fingertips
The skin under her fingernails
The canal inside her ear
questions.context: Unbroken skin, with its tough, dry outer layer of dead cells, is a barrier a cold virus cannot get through, pores and all, and the ear canal is lined with skin too. When she touched her nose, the virus on her fingers reached the moist lining inside, where cold viruses take hold; touching the face with unwashed hands is one of the main ways colds spread.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade defence lessons open with the skin as the first barrier, and germs getting in through the body's moist openings instead, the nose above all, is the case taught with it.

questions.question: The windpipe is lined with sticky mucus and with tiny hair-like parts called cilia, which beat together 10 to 20 times a second. Dust and germs breathed in get stuck in the mucus. Where do the beating cilia carry it?
choices: Up to the throat
Down into the lungs
Out through the nose
Into the blood
questions.context: The cilia sweep the mucus and its trapped germs up the windpipe to the throat, where it is swallowed or coughed up. Even the nose's own mucus is mostly moved backward by cilia and swallowed without anyone noticing, while the hairs just inside the nostrils catch the bigger bits of dust.
questions.grade_note: Mucus and cilia in the airways are the barrier 6th-grade lessons teach after the skin, and the job of the cilia, sweeping trapped germs out, is the simple why.

questions.question: A meal carries many bacteria into the body, yet most of them are dead before they reach the intestines. What kills most of them?
choices: Acid in the stomach
Bile from the liver
Heat inside the belly
Mucus in the food pipe
questions.context: The stomach's juices hold hydrochloric acid, strong enough to kill most of the bacteria and other germs that come in with food and drink, and the same acid helps digest the food. Bile does its work later, in the small intestine; the mucus of the food pipe eases food on its way; and many germs grow best at the body's own warmth.
questions.grade_note: Stomach acid killing swallowed germs is one of the barriers in the standard 6th-grade list of the body's first defences.

questions.question: Bacteria get into a cut on a boy's hand. Within hours, white blood cells squeeze out of the nearby blood vessels and reach the bacteria. How do many of these white blood cells destroy them?
questions.answer: They swallow them and digest them
choices: They swallow them and digest them
They seal them inside a blood clot
They take away all their oxygen
They coat them in sticky mucus
questions.context: Many white blood cells, called phagocytes, wrap themselves around a germ, take it inside and break it down. Clots are the work of platelets, carrying oxygen is the job of red blood cells, and mucus comes from the linings of the airways and the gut, not from white blood cells.
questions.grade_note: That white blood cells attack the germs that get past the barriers, many by engulfing them, is the core 6th-grade fact about them.

questions.question: A splinter stays in a girl's finger for a few days. The skin around it turns red, warm and swollen, and a spot of thick, yellowish pus forms under the skin. What is the pus mostly made of?
questions.answer: Dead and dying white blood cells
choices: Dead and dying white blood cells
Red blood cells that have gone bad
Fat leaking out from under the skin
Mucus made by the sore skin
questions.context: Pus is mostly neutrophils, the commonest white blood cells, which crowded into the finger to fight the bacteria and died there, in a fluid with broken-down tissue and germs. The redness and warmth come from extra blood flowing in, and the swelling from fluid and white blood cells leaving the blood vessels.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders learn that white blood cells gather and fight where germs get in, and pus and the red, swollen skin around a wound are the signs of that fight they can see.

questions.question: A boy with strep throat runs a fever of 39 degrees Celsius, and his forehead feels hot to his mother's hand. What makes his temperature rise?
questions.answer: His brain sets his body to run hotter
choices: His brain sets his body to run hotter
The bacteria give off heat as they grow
His sore throat heats the blood passing by
His body has lost control of its heat
questions.context: A fever is one of the body's own defences: chemicals from white blood cells turn up the temperature control centre in the brain, and the body makes heat, often by shivering at first, to reach the new setting. The extra heat slows many germs and speeds up white blood cells. A body that has truly lost control of its heat, as in heatstroke, is overheating, not running a fever.
questions.grade_note: Fever as one of the body's defences, turned up by the body itself rather than made by the germs, is taught with the 6th-grade immune system, and its job of slowing germs is the simple why.

questions.question: A girl with a cold feels tender lumps on both sides of her neck, under the jaw. They are lymph nodes, small bean-shaped organs that people often call glands. Why have they swollen?
questions.answer: White blood cells in them are multiplying
choices: White blood cells in them are multiplying
Mucus from her nose is draining into them
They are making extra spit for her throat
The cold virus has spread to her neck's skin
questions.context: Lymph nodes filter the fluid called lymph, trap germs and hold many white blood cells. Near an infection those white blood cells multiply, and more crowd in to fight it, so the nodes swell into the lumps people call swollen glands; they go down within a week or two.
questions.grade_note: The lymph nodes, where white blood cells gather, and why they swell in an illness are part of the lymphatic system the 6th-grade body unit teaches.

questions.question: A girl had chickenpox when she was five. Years later her little brother catches it, and though she plays with him every day, she stays well. Why does she not catch it again?
questions.answer: Her body remembers the germ and stops it fast
choices: Her body remembers the germ and stops it fast
She has grown too old to catch that germ
Her skin has grown too thick for that germ
The germ grows weaker as it passes between people
questions.context: Beating chickenpox left her body with memory cells and antibodies made for that one germ. When it came again, her defences knew it and stopped it before it could make her ill, which is why most people have chickenpox only once. Age is no shield: a grown-up who has never had it can catch it, and it spreads to as many as nine in ten people at home who have never had it.
questions.grade_note: That the body remembers a germ it has beaten, so that most people catch chickenpox only once, is the 6th-grade fact about immunity after an illness.

questions.question: A boy catches a cold in October and another in January. His body remembers germs it has beaten, yet he catches cold after cold, year after year. Why does that memory not protect him?
questions.answer: Colds come from many different viruses
choices: Colds come from many different viruses
Cold weather wipes out the body's memory
The body's memory works only on bacteria
His first cold was never fully beaten
questions.context: More than 200 different viruses cause colds, and beating one protects only against that one, so a new cold is usually a virus his body has never met. The memory works on viruses as well as bacteria (measles, a virus, usually leaves protection for life), a cold is over in about a week to ten days, and cold weather does not cause colds: they are commoner in winter because people crowd together indoors.
questions.grade_note: That the body's memory is for one particular germ, so a new cold virus can still make a person ill, follows directly from the 6th-grade lesson on immunity.

questions.question: Health experts say to scrub the hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Soap and scrubbing get rid of many more germs than water alone. Why does the soap help?
questions.answer: It lifts germs off for water to rinse away
choices: It lifts germs off for water to rinse away
It closes the skin's pores to keep germs out
It leaves a coating that germs cannot stick to
It draws out germs hiding deep in the skin
questions.context: Soap loosens the grease and dirt that germs cling to, and with the rubbing of scrubbing it lifts them off the skin so the water can carry them away, soap and all. Warm and cold water work about as well, and teaching people to wash this way cuts the number who catch colds or come down with diarrhoea.
questions.grade_note: Hand-washing as the everyday way to remove germs before they reach the body is taught with the 6th-grade defences, and soap's job is the simple why.
